thread.title: Shareholders could get a $1 trillion present from companies in 2018 - MarketWatch

author: Ryan Vlastelica
title: Shareholders could get a $1 trillion present from companies in 2018 - MarketWatch

organizations.name: courtesy everett collection ryan vlastelica markets

text:
Published: Mar 21, 2018 11:43 a.m. ET Share 
Buybacks grew in the fourth quarter and dividends hit a record Courtesy Everett Collection Ryan Vlastelica Markets reporter 
U.S. companies, the biggest source of demand on Wall Street for buying stocks , continue to have a voracious appetite for their own shares. 
According to S&P Dow Jones Indices, companies in the S&P 500 SPX, +0.26% spent $137 billion on buyback programs in the fourth quarter of 2017, a rate that was up 1.2% from the fourth quarter of 2016 and up 6% from the third quarter. ‘Buybacks and dividends could put the S&P 500 over $1 trillion for total shareholder return this year’ —Howard Silverblatt, senior index analyst at S&P Dow Jones Indices 
This growth is expected to only accelerate from here, as a highly anticipated tax-reform bill was passed in late December, giving a windfall to companies that is widely expected to be largely returned to shareholders in the form of repurchasing programs and dividends. According to TrimTabs Investment Research, new buybacks have totaled $226.6 billion thus far in 2018, a rate that represents sequential growth of 65.4% with more than a week left in the first quarter. 
“The average daily volume of announced corporate buying of $5.4 billion is not far below the record $5.8 billion daily in 2015,” TrimTabs wrote, referring to both buybacks and cash acquisitions. On an annualized basis, the firm added, this amounts to $1.35 trillion in such uses. “We doubt companies will be using anywhere near $1.35 trillion to hire or boost compensation this year. Like the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy, the federal government’s tax policy has become a major driver of inequality.” 
Excluding mergers and acquisitions, “buybacks and dividends could put the S&P 500 over $1 trillion for total shareholder return this year,” said Howard Silverblatt, Senior Index Analyst at S&P Dow Jones Indices. 
Related: Why the Disney deal suggests the tax bill may mean little for the economy 
In the fourth quarter, as well as for 2017 overall, financial companies were among the most aggressive repurchasers. Three of the five issues with the highest buyback totals were banks: Citigroup Inc. C, +0.27% spent $5.5 billion in the quarter, while Bank of America BAC, -0.22% bought back $4.9 billion and J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. JPM, +0.39% repurchased $4.81 billion of its own stock. Overall, financials spent $33.9 billion on buybacks in the quarter, accounting for 24.8% of total buybacks. 
The biggest repurchaser, however, was Apple Inc. AAPL, -0.72% the largest company in the economy by market capitalization. The tech giant spent $10.1 billion on buybacks in the quarter, the 12th-highest quarter in S&P 500 history, according to the data. Apple’s heavy purchasing contributed to tech being the sector with the most buybacks; the industry accounted for 26.1% of the index’s total buybacks. 
Despite this, repurchasing stocks was a popular ploy for companies regardless of sector. According to S&P Dow Jones Indices, 294 of the S&P 500’s components reduced their share count during the fourth quarter, compared with 281 in the year-ago period and 274 in the third quarter of 2017. However, only 70 companies reduced their share count by at least 4%; that is the level that is seen as having a measurable effect on improving profits. (Because profits are measured in earnings per share, reducing the number of shares outstanding has the same impact, mathematically, as increasing revenue.) 
Beyond buybacks, dividend payouts hit a record $109.5 billion in the fourth quarter, up 3.8% from the third quarter. The average dividend increase was 14.04%. Total shareholder returns were $246.4 billion in the fourth quarter, up 5% from the previous quarter. Related Topics
